title.en: Language work for Follow That Dream: -scape nouns, idioms, conditionals and Latin phrases in English

text.en: In Follow That Dream and Believe in Yourself, every dreamer moves past comfort and fear into action. Unit 8 builds words ending in -scape, teaches vivid idioms about determination, sharpens conditional sentences with imperatives, and decodes common Latin expressions used in everyday English.

Notice the compound noun 'dreamscape' in the chapter. The suffix-like root '-scape' comes from 'landscape' and means a view, scene, or wide mental picture.
Practise the four '-scape' words from the Sneha-Kiran dialogue: 'seascape' depicts coastal ocean views (Goa beaches), while 'cityscape' shows bustling urban skylines and streets.
'Landscape' pictures natural landforms like forests and hills, whereas 'mindscape' describes the inner world of thoughts and imagination.
Unit 8 highlights six colourful expressions in context. A dream that 'burns in your blood' is a passionate desire you refuse to abandon, while 'an uphill task' is a genuinely tough challenge.
'Buoyed up' means lifted in spirit and encouraged by success, while 'coursing through her veins' shows an emotion surging strongly throughout her.
Contrast 'wishful thinking'—a hopeful guess unlikely to succeed without real effort—with 'a wet blanket'—a spoil-sport person who dampens everyone else's enthusiasm.
Look closely at the conditional grammar pattern: 'If the burning conviction is still coursing through your veins, then go ahead and do something about it.'
Instead of writing 'will + verb' in the main clause, conditional sentences giving advice or commands use an imperative verb ('go ahead', 'stay focused', 'keep trying').
In the second grammar focus, Unit 8 reviews present versus past-participle forms and active reasoning: verbs agree with their true subjects across classroom debates and project paragraphs.
Now look at 'status quo' in both the story and poem 'Believe in Yourself'. 'Status quo' is a Latin phrase meaning the existing state of affairs when things stay unchanged.
English borrows several everyday Latin abbreviations and phrases: 'et cetera (etc.)' means and other similar things, while 'exempli gratia (e.g.)' introduces an example.
'Ad hoc' names something arranged for a specific temporary purpose, whereas 'per se' means by itself or fundamentally ('Writing is not hard per se, though editing takes patience').
Learn the final two Latin phrases in the table: 'in media res' means starting a story right in the middle of action, and 'quid pro quo' means a favour or exchange given in return for something.
Notice the Unit 8 tasks too: an enquiry email to a design institute director (clear subject, formal tone, specific course/fee questions) and an open-ended persuasive speech urging peers not to fear stepping out of comfort zones.

board.text: in media res & quid pro quo

text.en: Notice the Unit 8 tasks too: an enquiry email to a design institute director (clear subject, formal tone, specific course/fee questions) and an open-ended persuasive speech urging peers not to fear stepping out of comfort zones.

problem.en: Pick the right Latin expression and conditional form: (a) Ritu helped Tanya and then asked for help in return—a fair ___. (b) If you want to grow, ___ (avoid) staying comfortable.

why.en: 'Quid pro quo' means something given in return for an earlier favour.
Using an imperative verb ('avoid') in the main clause gives clear advice after 'If + present simple'.

prompt.en: Explain four Latin phrases taught in Unit 8 and show how an imperative works inside a conditional sentence.

requiredIdeas.en: status quo: existing unchanged state; etc.: and other things; e.g.: for example
ad hoc: temporary specific purpose; in media res: starting in the middle; quid pro quo: favour in return
If + present clause followed by an imperative main clause gives practical instruction or encouragement

commonMisconceptions.en: Confusing e.g. (for example) with etc. (and other things)

points.en: -scape compounds picture scenes: seascape (sea), landscape (land), cityscape (city), mindscape (inner thoughts).
Idioms: uphill task (tough challenge), buoyed up (encouraged), wishful thinking (unrealistic hope), wet blanket (spoil-sport).
If + simple present + imperative ('go ahead', 'step up') expresses strong advice or encouragement.
Latin terms in English: status quo, etc., e.g., ad hoc, per se, in media res, quid pro quo.
